hook.support: This is your project. You pick it. It can be about a job, a skill, a cause or your town. First, you pitch it. Then you plan it. Then you make it better with feedback.
hook.core: This one’s yours. A project about something you actually care about: a job you want, a skill you’re good at, a cause, a club, your town. Before you start, you’ll pitch it to your teacher, plan how you’ll present it, and make the plan better with feedback. Good projects start with a good pitch.
hook.extend: Your Project is the biggest piece of work in VPC Literacy, and you choose it. Strong projects start with a narrow, interesting focus, a negotiated agreement with your teacher, early research and a presentation plan that’s been tested on real people. This course gets all of that done before you build anything.

why.support: A clear plan makes a big project easy. Feedback early saves you work later.
why.core: Big projects go wrong at the start: the topic is too big, or the plan is fuzzy. A clear pitch, early research and feedback save you hours later. It’s also how real projects work in jobs.
why.extend: Negotiating a scope, planning a deliverable and refining it after feedback are core workplace skills. Getting them right at the start is what separates projects that finish well from projects that stall.

articles.title: Pick it, pitch it, plan it

body.support:
Your project is about something **you** care about. It could be a job, a skill, a cause, a club or your town. You can work alone or in a group.

**1. Pick it.** Choose a topic. Then make it **narrow**. “Cars” is too big. “How to fix up my first car” is a project.

**2. Pitch it.** Tell your teacher:
- what your project is.
- why it matters to you.
- who it’s for.
- how you’ll show it (slides, a video, a poster).

Talk until you both agree.

**3. Research it.** Find **three good sources**. A website, a video, or a person you talk to. Write short notes on each one. Keep them in your **portfolio**.

**4. Plan it.** Plan what you’ll say and show. Add body language notes, like “look up” and “slow down”.

**5. Test it.** Show your plan to others. Ask what to **keep**, **change** and **add**. Then fix your plan.
body.core:
Your Project is about something **you** care about: a job you want, a skill you have, a cause, a club, a place. You can work alone or in a small group.

**1. Pick it, then narrow it.** Start with an interest, then turn it into a **focus question**. “Cars” is a topic. “What does it really cost to get my first car on the road?” is a project. A narrow focus is easier to research and much more interesting to listen to.

**2. Pitch it.** Meet with your teacher and pitch your idea:
- **What** is your project and focus question?
- **Why** does it matter to you?
- **Who** is your audience?
- **How** will you show it: slides, a video, a poster, a demonstration?
- **What help** do you need?
.
This is a **negotiation**. Your teacher may suggest changes. Agree on a version you’re both happy with.

**3. Research it.** Find at least **three good sources**: websites, videos, reports, or an interview with someone who knows. For each one, write a short summary in your own words and note where it came from. These notes go in your **portfolio**.

**4. Plan the presentation.** Plan each part: what you’ll say, what you’ll show, and how you’ll deliver it. Use what you learnt in Body Talk: mark where you’ll look up, pause and slow down.

**5. Test the plan.** Show it to a few classmates. Ask them: what should I **keep**, **change** and **add**? Then refine your plan. Feedback now saves hours later.
body.extend:
Your Project is the major piece of work in VPC Literacy, and the topic is yours: a career pathway, a skill, a cause, a community group or a local issue, alone or in a small group.

**1. Develop a focus.** Move from a broad interest to a **focus question** you can actually answer. “Cars” is a topic; “What does it really cost a 17-year-old to get a first car on the road?” is a project. Narrow focus makes research manageable and presentations sharper.

**2. Negotiate it.** Pitch a short proposal to your teacher covering the what (focus question), why (personal relevance), who (audience), how (presentation format and digital support) and what support you’ll need. Expect questions and suggested changes; the goal is an agreed scope you can realistically complete.

**3. Build a research portfolio.** Locate at least **three credible sources** of different kinds (written, multimedia, an interview with someone experienced). For each, write a brief **annotation**: what it says, why it’s useful, and how reliable it is, with the full source recorded. This is the evidence base for your presentation, and it makes acknowledging sources easy later.

**4. Plan the presentation.** Sequence the content logically and plan the delivery: where you’ll use visuals, and deliberate body language, eye contact, pace and pauses (from Body Talk).

**5. Refine after feedback.** Test the plan on peers using a simple protocol (keep, change, add), then revise. Treat feedback as data, not criticism: it shows you how a real audience will experience your presentation.

caseStudies.title: The caravan project

body.support:
In 2023, Year 11 students at **Castlemaine Secondary College** started a project. It was called **Caravan Fix Me Up**.

The students were doing **VM, VCAL and FLO** programs.

They found an old, broken-down caravan. With help from local tradies, they fixed it up.

The caravan would give a family facing **homelessness** somewhere to stay for a while.

The students learned real trade skills. They also helped their own town.
body.core:
In 2023, Year 11 students at **Castlemaine Secondary College**, in central Victoria, took on a project called **Caravan Fix Me Up**. They were in the school’s **VM, VCAL and FLO** programs.

The plan was simple. Take a run-down caravan and fix it up. Then it could give families facing **homelessness** in their area a place to stay for a while.

The school didn’t do it alone. A local health service, **Dhelkaya Health**, helped. So did a group of local tradies called **HALT**, a local network that links schools with work, and local suppliers.

The students got hands-on trade skills. They worked with real tradies. And they made something their town needed.
body.extend:
In 2023, Year 11 students in the **VM, VCAL and FLO** programs at **Castlemaine Secondary College**, in central Victoria, ran a project called **Caravan Fix Me Up**. They restored a run-down caravan, so it could give families facing **homelessness** in their area a place to stay.

Two things made it work: a clear, practical focus and the right partners. The school worked with a local health service (**Dhelkaya Health**), a group of local tradies (**HALT**), a network that links schools with work, and local suppliers. Students gained real trade skills working alongside professionals. The result met a real local need.

It’s a useful model for any project. Have one specific goal (one caravan, one purpose). Have a real audience, and someone who benefits. And find people outside the classroom who can help.

model.text:
**Focus question:** What is a day really like for a vet nurse?

**Why me:** I want to work with animals after school.

**Audience:** my class, and Year 10s choosing their pathway.

**How I’ll show it:** five slides with photos, plus a short video of an interview with a vet nurse.

**Sources so far:**
1. Your Career website: the vet nurse job page.
2. A TAFE page for the Certificate IV in Veterinary Nursing.
3. An interview with Jess, a vet nurse at our local clinic.

**Feedback I got:** “Keep the interview. Change: fewer slides. Add: what you’d earn.”

**What I changed:** I cut to four slides and added a pay slide.

teacher.overview: The first Your Project course (VPC Unit 4 Module 1). Students turn an interest into a focus question, pitch and negotiate their project with you, build an annotated research portfolio of at least three sources, plan the presentation (content, visuals and delivery cues), and refine the plan after structured peer feedback (keep, change, add). The case study is Castlemaine Secondary College’s 2023 Caravan Fix Me Up project, run by VM, VCAL and FLO students with local partners. Showcase Day is where the project is presented.
prep: Block out 5-minute pitch conferences with every student (a lesson for a class of 20).
Prepare a list of local contacts students might interview: employers, clubs, council youth services.
Decide whether group projects are allowed and how individual contributions will be shown.

teacher.answers:
**Sort:** cars — too broad; netball lights — clear; music — too broad; dog-walking business — clear; sport — too broad; vet nurse day — clear.

**Annotation:** 1 focus question (narrow, answerable); 2 why it matters personally; 3 audience; 4 format and digital support; 5 a mix of sources; 6 support needed from the teacher.

**Case study:** restoring a caravan for temporary accommodation for families facing homelessness; Dhelkaya Health, HALT local tradies, the Goldfields LLEN and suppliers provided skills and materials; a narrow practical goal with real partners and a real need.

realityCheck: **Topic choice is where projects succeed or fail.** Spend the time on narrowing. A student with a clear question in week 1 will finish; a student with “cars” won’t.
**Pitch conferences take time.** Five minutes each adds up. Run them while the rest of the class researches.
**Interviews are gold but need care.** Check students know how to contact adults safely and politely, and that a staff member knows who they’re meeting.
**Group projects need individual evidence.** If students work together, each keeps their own portfolio and presents a part.
**Works in a real class:** yes, and choice is the engine. Students who’ve disengaged elsewhere often invest heavily in a topic they picked.

levels.support: Aimed at about Year 5 reading: shorter article and case study, 6 key words, word bank, a teacher list of focus questions, and two sources plus an interview.
levels.core: Aimed at about Year 7 reading: the standard version with focus questions, negotiation, a three-source portfolio, a presentation plan and keep-change-add feedback.
levels.extend: Aimed at about Year 9 reading: scope negotiation, annotations that judge reliability, feedback as data, and a group portfolio check.
